Content:
Every linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] that acts on 2D-vectors has a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: T] associated with it. The matrix is called the standard matrix of the linear transformation.
For any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the standard matrix [MATH: T] of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] must have the property

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = T \cdot \mathbf{v}]

Content:
where [MATH: T \cdot \mathbf{v}] is the matrix product of the standard matrix [MATH: T] and the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
To illustrate, consider the following linear transformation:

Content:
[MATH: [x; y]]

Content:
The standard matrix for the linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{S}] is [MATH: [− 3|7; 1|− 5]] since it has the following property:

Content:
[MATH: [− 3|7; 1|− 5]^(⏞)^(S) ⋅ [x; y]|= [− 3 ⋅ x + 7 ⋅ y; 1 ⋅ x + (− 5) ⋅ y]; = [− 3x + 7y; x − 5y]; = S[x; y].]

Content:
Notice here that [MATH: \mathbf{S}] (using a bold letter) denotes the transformation (function) itself, while [MATH: S] (big italic letter) is a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix that corresponds to the linear transformation.

Content:
In general, the standard matrix of the linear transformation [MATH: [x; y]] is
[MATH: [a|b; c|d]]

Content:
We can learn a lot about linear transformations by looking at their standard matrices.
